brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

profile.description:
Xplor Recreation is the name the company uses for itself throughout nextrec.com: the support menu offers "How you can get in touch with Xplor Recreation", the demo form states that "Xplor Recreation uses the information you provide to us to contact you about our relevant content, products, and services", and xplorrecreation.com serves pages out of the same site. The product behind the name is nextRec, which the homepage describes as "Frictionless all-in-one parks and recreation management software that lets your clients easily self serve their needs". The solutions menu sells it to parks and recreation departments, cities, municipalities, community centers, YMCAs and JCCs; universities, colleges and K-12 schools; community, residents' and homeowners' associations; summer, day and specialized camps; martial arts dojos and MMA gyms; and swim schools. The parks and recreation page says the software "helps municipalities and government organizations of all sizes connect with their community" and covers "managing operations, payment processing, membership management, and program coordination". The named modules are Member Management, Calendar and Bookings, Marketing Automation, POS and Payments, Facility Management, Citywide POS ("One-stop-shop to consolidate payments"), Mobile App, Court Booking System, Queue-it ("A virtual waiting room system to support extreme web traffic events") and Kiosks. Facility Management covers "indoor and outdoor facilities, parks, fields, campgrounds, meeting spaces, party venues", and reporting covers "financial reporting, facility usage, daily operations". The site lists existing integrations with payment providers, financial systems, automated lighting systems, GIS, access controls and directory services, plus a RESTful API.

Xplor's own corporate site groups four brands under the Xplor Recreation heading: Vermont Systems, RecDesk, NextRec and CampBrain. ePACT is not among them on that page. nextrec.com closes with "Copyright 2026 Xplor Technologies. All rights reserved." and links to linkedin.com/company/xplor-technologies. On scale, nextrec.com states that Xplor Technologies "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe"; the parks and recreation page separately claims 21+ countries, 500,000+ users and 150+ employees, and 24-hour support seven days a week. Named public-sector customers quoted on that page are Andre W. of the City of Pearland, TX, Alex N. of Roanoke County, VA, and Anand P. of the City of Brampton, ON, who says "We've had 95% of people switch to online. Previously it was predominantly in-person registration." The platform is hosted on Amazon Web Services in Australia, the United States and Canada, is described as PCI-DSS Level 1 certified, and carries a 99.95% uptime guarantee. Within the family, this is the brand that carries the all-in-one registration-and-facilities system; the sibling products under the same owner are addressed at different sizes and kinds of agency.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

brands.name: RecDesk
brands.description:
recdesk.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear on repeated attempts. No attempt was made to defeat it, so nothing below comes from RecDesk's own site. What follows is from Xplor's corporate site, which is the family's own material. Xplor writes: "Founded in 2005, RecDesk provides scalable, easy-to-use software for parks and recreation departments, aquatic centers, schools, community centers, HOAs, and small municipalities. Its integrations with access control, GIS/address databases, and financial systems help teams streamline facility scheduling, program management, and operational workflows - reducing manual effort and system fragmentation." Xplor adds that "Business and community leaders can run more efficient programs, offer better resident experiences, and make data-driven decisions that strengthen their community services."

RecDesk is one of the four brands Xplor lists on its Xplor Recreation page, alongside Vermont Systems, NextRec and CampBrain, and Xplor's "Visit RecDesk" link points to recdesk.com. The distinction Xplor's own wording draws between the siblings is the size and type of buyer: RecDesk is described for "small municipalities", aquatic centers and HOAs, where Vermont Systems is described for "municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations". RecDesk's postings run through the Rippling board shared across this family, clubessential-holdings-cjb, which also carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. Beyond that, this record is deliberately short. Anything further about RecDesk's product, customers or scale would have to be invented, because its site refused to be read.

brands.name: Vermont Systems
brands.description:
vermontsystems.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear. No attempt was made to defeat it. Everything below comes from other pages inside the same family. Xplor's corporate site says: "Founded in 1985, Vermont Systems is a leading recreation management platform built for municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations. Its comprehensive operational, payment, and experience-management features help teams simplify daily tasks, modernize processes, and reduce manual work." ePACT, a sibling brand, describes it twice on its own site: "We have partnered with Vermont Systems, a market leader in recreation management software for parks & recreation, schools, and governments", and, using the company's initials, "We integrate with VSI, a market leader in recreation management software for parks & recreation, schools, and governments." ePACT also names the flagship product, listing RecTrac beside ActiveNet and Daxko as the registration systems it plugs into.

Within the family, the federal military recreation buyer is the piece no sibling claims: Xplor's description of Vermont Systems is the only one of the four that reaches past local government to "state, and federal military recreation organizations", where RecDesk is described for "small municipalities" and NextRec for "sports, leisure, and recreation centers, clubs, communities, and federations". Vermont Systems is also the one recreation brand Xplor names in its general hiring boilerplate: postings on the shared Rippling board, clubessential-holdings-cjb, open "Xplor Technologies powers the experiences at the heart of everyday life" and go on, "We unite popular brands such as Clubessential, foreUP, myFitApp, Vermont Systems, Momence, Exerp, and many more." That same board carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. Nothing about Vermont Systems' customer count, staff or current product line is recorded here, because its own site was unreadable.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "PowerDMS by NEOGOV" DUPLICATE RECORD - board ids 'power-dms-by-neogov' and 'powerdms-by-neogov' are ONE COMPANY recorded twice. Same vendor, same product, same domain; the only difference is the spacing in the name ('Power DMS' vs 'PowerDMS'). These need MERGING into a single record, not two copies of the same website. URL itself verifies: fetched https://www.powerdms.com, which is live and carries 'PowerDMS by NEOGOV' branding in both header and footer, and sells 'PowerPolicy' for policy management and 'PowerStandards' for accreditation management, helping agencies 'manage, maintain, and prove agency-wide compliance' - matching the description exactly. Rule 3 satisfied: powerdms.com is the acquired brand's OWN domain, not the parent's corporate site (neogov.com is only a nav link out to 'NEOGOV - Public Sector HR Solutions'). WARNING for the board's scraper: powerdms.com/careers does not host PowerDMS jobs itself - it links out to NEOGOV's shared portal at https://www.governmentjobs.com/careers/neogovpe. Scraping that careers path will return NEOGOV-wide postings, which reintroduces the exact misattribution rule 3 is meant to prevent. Job ingestion should filter to PowerDMS/Orlando roles.

Simpleview was acquired by Granicus (press release 2026-09-05 on granicus.com) and Granicus's destinations FAQ answers "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" with "Yes". The solutions site stays at simpleviewinc.com for now - "The two websites will be combined in the near future" - so the brand keeps its own website here.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© Copyright 2026 Concur Technologies, Inc. All rights reserved." Fetched https://www.concur.com (curl with browser UA, HTTP 200, 170KB; WebFetch got 403 so I used curl). Page title: "Spend Management Software for Travel, Expense, Invoice | SAP Concur", canonical https://www.concur.com/. Rule 3 check PASSED: this is NOT sap.com. It is the brand's own domain, copyright held by Concur Technologies, Inc., with its own product navigation (Concur Expense, Concur Travel, Concur Invoice, Concur Request, Concur TripLink) and its own solutions nav including "Government", "Government contracting" and "State & local governments". Matches the description (travel, expense and invoice software). CAVEAT the board operator should know: https://www.concur.com/careers 302s off-domain to https://jobs.sap.com/search (unfiltered, all-SAP job search). So the URL is correct as the company's identity page, but any scraper that follows the careers link will inherit SAP's entire global req list rather than SAP Concur roles. Recommend the record carry the site but not auto-scrape jobs.sap.com/search unfiltered.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© Copyright 2026 Concur Technologies, Inc. All rights reserved." Fetched https://www.concur.com (curl with browser UA, HTTP 200, 170KB; WebFetch got 403 so I used curl). Page title: "Spend Management Software for Travel, Expense, Invoice | SAP Concur", canonical https://www.concur.com/. Rule 3 check PASSED: this is NOT sap.com. It is the brand's own domain, copyright held by Concur Technologies, Inc., with its own product navigation (Concur Expense, Concur Travel, Concur Invoice, Concur Request, Concur TripLink) and its own solutions nav including "Government", "Government contracting" and "State & local governments". Matches the description (travel, expense and invoice software). CAVEAT the board operator should know: https://www.concur.com/careers 302s off-domain to https://jobs.sap.com/search (unfiltered, all-SAP job search). So the URL is correct as the company's identity page, but any scraper that follows the careers link will inherit SAP's entire global req list rather than SAP Concur roles. Recommend the record carry the site but not auto-scrape jobs.sap.com/search unfiltered.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© Copyright 2026 Concur Technologies, Inc. All rights reserved." Fetched https://www.concur.com (curl with browser UA, HTTP 200, 170KB; WebFetch got 403 so I used curl). Page title: "Spend Management Software for Travel, Expense, Invoice | SAP Concur", canonical https://www.concur.com/. Rule 3 check PASSED: this is NOT sap.com. It is the brand's own domain, copyright held by Concur Technologies, Inc., with its own product navigation (Concur Expense, Concur Travel, Concur Invoice, Concur Request, Concur TripLink) and its own solutions nav including "Government", "Government contracting" and "State & local governments". Matches the description (travel, expense and invoice software). CAVEAT the board operator should know: https://www.concur.com/careers 302s off-domain to https://jobs.sap.com/search (unfiltered, all-SAP job search). So the URL is correct as the company's identity page, but any scraper that follows the careers link will inherit SAP's entire global req list rather than SAP Concur roles. Recommend the record carry the site but not auto-scrape jobs.sap.com/search unfiltered.

Fetched https://www.concur.com (curl with browser UA, HTTP 200, 170KB; WebFetch got 403 so I used curl). Page title: "Spend Management Software for Travel, Expense, Invoice | SAP Concur", canonical https://www.concur.com/. Rule 3 check PASSED: this is NOT sap.com. It is the brand's own domain, copyright held by Concur Technologies, Inc., with its own product navigation (Concur Expense, Concur Travel, Concur Invoice, Concur Request, Concur TripLink) and its own solutions nav including "Government", "Government contracting" and "State & local governments". Matches the description (travel, expense and invoice software). CAVEAT the board operator should know: https://www.concur.com/careers 302s off-domain to https://jobs.sap.com/search (unfiltered, all-SAP job search). So the URL is correct as the company's identity page, but any scraper that follows the careers link will inherit SAP's entire global req list rather than SAP Concur roles. Recommend the record carry the site but not auto-scrape jobs.sap.com/search unfiltered.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently" The URL is factually correct and does NOT violate the parent-domain rule: aws.amazon.com is AWS's own canonical property (its own brand, console, pricing, docs and its own careers page at https://aws.amazon.com/careers/, HTTP 200), not Amazon's corporate site at amazon.com. The govtech tie is on-domain too: https://aws.amazon.com/government-education/ (HTTP 200) is AWS's public sector page, and the homepage names 'AWS GovCloud (US-East)' and 'AWS GovCloud (US-West)'. MY JUDGMENT ON WHETHER THE BOARD SHOULD CARRY THIS AT ALL - the URL passes but the record is still risky, for a reason the URL check cannot fix: aws.amazon.com/careers/ does not host jobs, it hands off to https://www.amazon.jobs/en/business_categories/amazon-web-services. That feed is tens of thousands of global AWS engineering/PM/ops roles, of which SLED account executive roles are a tiny fraction. Any homepage- or careers-page-level scrape of this record will flood SLED JOBS with irrelevant listings - the same practical damage the parent-domain rule exists to prevent, arriving by a different route. Recommendation: keep the URL if AWS is wanted on the board, but the record must be wired to

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently" The URL is factually correct and does NOT violate the parent-domain rule: aws.amazon.com is AWS's own canonical property (its own brand, console, pricing, docs and its own careers page at https://aws.amazon.com/careers/, HTTP 200), not Amazon's corporate site at amazon.com. The govtech tie is on-domain too: https://aws.amazon.com/government-education/ (HTTP 200) is AWS's public sector page, and the homepage names 'AWS GovCloud (US-East)' and 'AWS GovCloud (US-West)'. MY JUDGMENT ON WHETHER THE BOARD SHOULD CARRY THIS AT ALL - the URL passes but the record is still risky, for a reason the URL check cannot fix: aws.amazon.com/careers/ does not host jobs, it hands off to https://www.amazon.jobs/en/business_categories/amazon-web-services. That feed is tens of thousands of global AWS engineering/PM/ops roles, of which SLED account executive roles are a tiny fraction. Any homepage- or careers-page-level scrape of this record will flood SLED JOBS with irrelevant listings - the same practical damage the parent-domain rule exists to prevent, arriving by a different route. Recommendation: keep the URL if AWS is wanted on the board, but the record must be wired to

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

That feed is tens of thousands of global AWS engineering/PM/ops roles, of which SLED account executive roles are a tiny fraction. Any homepage- or careers-page-level scrape of this record will flood SLED JOBS with irrelevant listings - the same practical damage the parent-domain rule exists to prevent, arriving by a different route. Recommendation: keep the URL if AWS is wanted on the board, but the record must be wired to

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

paragraphs: Verkada sells cloud-managed physical security systems that customers around the world use to operate safer, smarter buildings. The line covers cameras, alarms, and unified cloud physical security software with remote access and AI analytics. Customers control an entire physical security operation from Verkada Command.

More than 30,000 organizations worldwide use Verkada, from small and midsize businesses to Fortune 500 leaders. Customer stories include the City of Los Angeles, which uses Verkada to unify physical security and improve public safety. paragraphs: SoundThinking, Inc., listed on Nasdaq as SSTI, sells AI and data-driven public safety technology to law enforcement, civic leadership, and security professionals. The company reports more than 300 customers and work with approximately 2,100 agencies. Its SafetySmart Platform includes ShotSpotter, an acoustic gunshot detection system that detects and verifies gunfire incidents in near real time. The platform also includes CrimeTracer, a law enforcement search engine, and CaseBuilder, an investigation management system. ResourceRouter directs patrol and community anti-violence resources, and SafePointe is an AI-based weapons detection system. The company was founded as ShotSpotter in 1996 by physicist Dr. Robert Showen, who was then working on locating earthquake epicenters at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California. Ralph Clark was hired as CEO in 2010 and changed the model so the system was sold as a subscription rather than as a capital hardware purchase. He also set up a centralized Incident Review Center so that human review of potential gunshots was done in-house rather than by police departments. The gunshot detection service now serves over 170 cities. In 2023 the company rebranded from ShotSpotter to SoundThinking and launched the SafetySmart Platform.

paragraphs: Lexipol packages policy, training, wellness, reporting, and grant support for public safety agencies into a single system. Two attorneys who had also been law enforcement officers created the company in 2003. The named buyers run from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators.

The policy product supplies state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then keeps them current as laws and standards change. The LexOne platform assigns training tied to policy, flags licenses and credentials nearing expiration, and tracks data for reporting. Online courses are accredited by organizations such as IADLEST, POST, and CAPCE.

Field training software digitizes records and editable Daily Observation Reports with supervisor sign-off. Professional Services comes in three tiers, the middle one covering hands-on training for a policy manager and help refining up to 50 high-risk policies. Grant services add a searchable database of available grants plus consultation on writing applications.

paragraphs: Fortem Technologies builds radar systems and autonomous drones that guard airspace for military and civilian operations. The work spans C-UAS, ISR, perimeter security, airspace safety, and several emerging airborne markets.

Three product families make up the SkyDome System: TrueView sensors, DroneHunter interceptors, and SkyDome Manager software. The DroneHunter F700 performs mid-air captures autonomously, with a stated 85% success rate. SkyDome Manager is the airspace monitoring and counter-UAS command and control software behind those sensors.

Buyers described on the site include airports, treated as a target for drone-based attacks. Law enforcement agencies are another, as criminals begin using store-bought drones to commit serious felonies. Backers named by the company include Lockheed Martin, Toshiba, Boeing, DCVC, and Signia Venture Partners.

paragraphs: Niche Technology sells NicheRMS365, a records management system that police agencies use to share information and eliminate siloed systems. The company describes the product as capturing policing from the front line to the courtroom. Sworn officers in over 180 agencies worldwide use NicheRMS365. Staff have a combined total of more than 500 years of policing experience.

South Yorkshire Police announced plans to implement NicheRMS365 to modernize crime recording and strengthen data integrity. Durham Constabulary has selected NicheRMS365. Warwickshire Police has selected it as well. The Toronto Police Service picked NicheRMS365 as its records management system, and Orange County, New York was named a 2025 Government Experience Award Winner by the Center for Digital Government for its NicheRMS project.

It is wholly owned by its founders, who remain active in day-to-day operations. NicheRMS365 is available through the General Services Administration Information Technology Schedule 70. paragraphs: Off Duty Management administers off-duty work programs for law enforcement agencies, their officers, and community businesses. Its OfficerTRAK® platform handles Police, Fire, or EMS off-duty job requests. Officers clock in and out, view job history, and get real-time notifications in the OfficerTRAK® app. The businesses hiring officers request shifts, receive invoices, and pay online through a portal.

Off Duty Management charges nothing to agencies and officers. It takes on the financial risk of late or non-payment by the off-duty employer, and says officers and agencies are paid weekly regardless of customer payment status. The company reports partnering with over 200 primary agencies and 300 backup agencies across the nation.

In Arizona, it deploys trained SSO officers across jurisdictions to help school districts fill School Safety Officer shifts. The Arizona Department of Education sets a curriculum officers must complete to be eligible for those shifts. Superintendent Tom Horne extended that partnership with Off Duty Management through 2026. Retired Austin Police Chief Brian Manley joined the company as President.

paragraphs: SurePassID sells deploy-anywhere multi-factor authentication for IT/OT and critical infrastructure, deployable in the cloud, on-premise, or within air-gapped networks. paragraphs: Safience sells identity intelligence systems that look only for predefined threats, persons of interest, and missing persons, matched against a database sourced from law enforcement. Its Real-Time Threat and Victim Identification Systems, RTIS and RVIS, use edge sensors that capture a single still image rather than video or audio. Images that do not match a predefined profile are purged immediately, and the sensors store no data on the device. The company states that alerts follow within 60 seconds of a detection and that queries return in under 5 seconds.

The database holds 57.3M+ unique individuals and receives over 50,000 new records per day, drawn from published law enforcement records, agency JMS/RMS integrations, an OffenderWatch partnership, and missing-person records. The dataset grew from 5.4M to 57.3M+ verified identities in 5 years. Target sectors listed include airports and mass transit systems, banks and financial institutions, K-12 schools and universities, hospitals, group homes, and LTC facilities, and hotels.

A second product, eMotive, turns a one-time criminal background check into a continuous, FCRA-compliant alert system for employers, with written consent required from each monitored individual. Matching for eMotive is performed by a third-party, NIST-approved provider in an isolated environment. Biometrica holds the U.S. patent for System and Method for Continuous Biometric Monitoring.

paragraphs: Skopenow sells a suite of online research and security products that generate intelligence reports on entities for fraud, threat, crime and due diligence work. The platform fuses crime data, consumer records, news, media and other data points to identify emerging threats, fraud, connections and criminal activity. The product line consists of five products: Grid, Pre-Check, Workbench, Link Analysis and Rabbit. Link Analysis generates visual connections between entities to map networks, and the platform runs dozens of purpose-built models for identifying fraud and threat insights. Its situational awareness capabilities give security teams real-time data that fuses media, traffic cams, crime, news, satellite imagery and message boards in a single dashboard.

The home page lists global security teams, loss prevention teams and executive protection teams as the groups it serves, and the product is free to try. The company says it has partnered with Fortune 500 companies, large government and law enforcement agencies, the largest insurance carriers and media outlets. It reports working with over 1,500 customers from around the world.

Skopenow was built in 2015 to help organizations understand internet data. It is a Techstars company whose investors include Runway VP and Barbara Corcoran. The company hosts free monthly virtual trainings for OSINT professionals.

paragraphs: Paladin autonomously deploys drones to emergency incidents so that aerial views reach responders before the first unit arrives. The platform is meant for departments regardless of city size and integrates with dispatch workflows.

Paladin supplies the drone, the software, the data management platform and the FAA waivers a department needs to operate legally. Its drone for emergency response, the Knighthawk, is made in the United States. The company describes that drone as NDAA approved and autonomous. paragraphs: Amped Software develops software for the analysis and enhancement of images and videos for forensic, security and investigative applications. Amped FIVE covers forensic image and video enhancement, while Amped Authenticate tests whether digital images and videos are reliable and admissible in court. Amped DVRConv converts batches of unplayable video files from proprietary CCTV and DVR formats, dash cams and body-worn cameras.

The tools are used for multimedia forensics in public safety and national security in over 100 countries. That customer base is put at more than 1500 organizations and more than 6000 licenses and seats sold. Training courses give hands-on instruction on the products and on forensic video and digital multimedia evidence processing.

Martino Jerian founded Amped Software in 2008 in Trieste, Italy, after graduating in Electronic Engineering at the University of Trieste. A subsidiary was established in Brooklyn, NY, as Amped Software USA Inc. The team numbers 41 people from 9 different countries, including former law enforcement officers and military.

paragraphs: AirSight sells a drone detection software platform called AirGuard that gives security teams the real-time location of drones and of their pilots. Detection layers offered are Remote ID, RF and DF, radar and camera. The company does not build the sensors itself and describes itself as a software and systems integration business that sources hardware from partners.

The site describes buyers including airports, stadiums, prisons, universities, army bases and Fortune 500 companies. Case files name the University of Kentucky, Camping World Stadium and the Chula Vista Police Department, whose own drone flights get third-party tracking. A Complete Tier adds radar for drones that do not transmit signals, plus staff who visually confirm alerts around the clock.

AirSight was established in 2003 as 911Security. Robert Tabbara, its President and Owner, started the business after the attacks of 9/11 2001. The move into drone detection software came in July 2019. Headquarters is in Dallas, TX, with offices in Chicago, IL and Pune, India, and the company is a registered Small Business Enterprise and Public Works Contractor.

paragraphs: Berkeley Varitronics Systems is a privately owned family business that has delivered custom wireless RF engineering products and solutions since 1972. It sells wireless security, detection and testing equipment to law enforcement, government and critical infrastructure buyers. The instruments detect covert cell phones, BLE tags, skimmers and rogue wireless devices.

BVS has designed, manufactured and shipped its own branded products from a headquarters in Metuchen, NJ since 1990, and the catalog has grown to some 200 unique products. PocketHound, a covert phone detector, has sold in the thousands to law enforcement, universities and correctional facilities. TransitHound, a cellular detection system built for mass transit, has been deployed in over 15,000 locomotives.

BVS also worked with law enforcement to unveil card skimmer detection products such as Skim Scan, Skim Swipe and BlueSleuth-Pro. Its clients range from NASA to Fortune 500 companies and small entrepreneurs seeking rapid development and prototyping.

paragraphs: Veritone sells enterprise AI software that converts unstructured video, audio, and text into data for models and automated workflows, across commercial media, public sector, and talent acquisition lines. Its aiWARE platform is described as a customizable platform configured to an organization's needs.

For government, legal, and education organizations, Veritone iDEMS is a digital evidence management system made up of five Veritone applications. Veritone Investigate acts as a central hub where an agency stores digital evidence from disparate locations, and Veritone Redact automates redaction of sensitive data from audio, video, and image-based evidence. Veritone Tracker tracks persons of interest across videos using similarity scores rather than facial recognition, and Veritone Illuminate searches Electronically Stored Information for early case assessment. Veritone Contact collects and reports stop data for California AB 953 Racial Identity and Profiling Act (RIPA) compliance, and Veritone IDentify uses a booking database to identify subjects. The home page cites the Pasadena Police Department, which the company says cut two weeks of redaction time to two days.

Commercial products Digital Media Hub, Discovery, Commerce, and Data Refinery serve media and sports organizations with asset tagging, search, and licensing. Veritone Hire lets talent acquisition teams advertise jobs through a single vendor integrated with over 120 applicant tracking systems and over 2000 publishers. The company also states it renewed and expanded an exclusive global licensing agreement with CBS News and Stations.

paragraphs: Tranquility AI makes AI-powered evidence analysis software for criminal investigations. Its flagship product, TimePilot, unifies all data sources into a single interface so investigators can surface details quickly. The company describes its technology as serving the entire justice system, from law enforcement to prosecuting attorneys.

For law enforcement, TimePilot is pitched at agencies of all sizes as a way to streamline investigation workflows and accelerate case clearance. Listed capabilities include processing months of data in minutes, building case timelines and generating case summaries. Featured investigation categories include homicides, cold cases, human trafficking, gangs, cyber crimes, domestic violence and cartel operations. For prosecutors, the company says using TimePilot cuts the average time to negotiate a plea from 30 days to 3 days.

The company page lists its Founder & CEO alongside a prior role as Technical Director for Counterterrorism at NSA, and other leaders with backgrounds at BlueVoyant, the Colorado Springs Police Department and the Chester County Sheriff's Office. Testimonials on the site come from a District Attorney in Orleans Parish, Louisiana, Sheriff Max Dorsey of Chester County, South Carolina, and Sheriff Ryan Spurling of Mason County, Washington. A detective at the Adams County Sheriffs Office in Colorado says the tool helped lead to an arrest and additional charges in one of that detective's cases.

paragraphs: NDI Recognition Systems sells Automatic License Plate Recognition products to law enforcement agencies worldwide. The same products are positioned for homeland security, where the company says they deliver data and recognition technology for defense analysis and prevention. Commercial uses include city parking ordinances, private and public parking garages and gas stations, and NDI also works with HOAs.

The company says it has worked with cities and countries securing borders, with technology built to perform 24/7 in harsh weather. NDI describes what it offers as a turnkey solution for all of a customer's ALPR needs.

A chief in South Carolina credits the ALPR with an arrest of individuals who broke into 25 cars. A crime analyst in Florida says camera data combined with witness statements, surveillance footage and DMV databases helped solve crimes.

provenance.quote: Our ALPR product solutions help law enforcement agencies worldwide prevent crime and protect their city borders.
NDI ALPR product solutions help defend the nation by delivering vital data and recognition technology for defense analysis and prevention.

Commercial ALPR uses are ideal for reinforcing city parking ordinances, private and public parking garages, and monitoring high-crime targets such as, gas stations. NDI also partners with HOAs to reduce neighborhood crime and congestion.

NDI Recognition Systems® has collaborated with both cities and countries looking to secure their borders with the very best in License Plate Recognition technology. ALPR Technology that could withstand the harshest weather conditions and still perform 24/7.
NDI Recognition Systems® is proud to offer our customers a turnkey solution for all their ALPR needs.
We have had many successes with the ALPR, including the arrest last week of individuals who broke into 25 cars last week & stole one of them.

paragraphs: Kaseware sells an investigation management platform that centralizes investigative details and case management so teams can close more cases. The buyers are corporate security teams, law enforcement, government agencies, and enterprise organizations with complex investigative or compliance needs. Built-in link analysis and geospatial tools surface connections and trends across investigative data.

Former FBI Special Agents founded Kaseware, bringing decades of public service and corporate software development experience. They had built Sentinel, which later became the foundation for Kaseware, a platform for incident responsiveness, case management, operations, and record keeping. The company states that more than 30% of the nation's fusion centers, agencies in all 50 US states, and businesses across the globe use Kaseware. DeliverFund is named as a client fighting human trafficking with combined resources and data.

Kaseware describes itself as CJIS-aligned and SOC2 Type 2 certified, with FedRAMP in progress. A GraphQL-based API supports integrations with OSINT tools, data analytics platforms, HR systems, and regulatory databases. Most deployments can be completed in 3 to 6 months using a phased train-the-trainer approach.

paragraphs: FaceTec sells face verification software that organizations use to confirm a remote user is real and physically present, both at account onboarding and on later logins. The company's stated best practice is for customers to keep users' biometric data, as 3D FaceMap or 3D FaceVector records, on their own servers, which run FaceTec's software inside the customer's firewall.

A related product, UR Codes, carries digitally signed biometric data so a codeholder can prove legal identity and age both in person and remotely. FaceTec says it trained its 3D algorithms with the help of over half a million volunteer testers from over 180 countries. It lists more than 90 channel partners worldwide.

paragraphs: Robin Radar Systems makes 360 degree, 3D radar systems that detect, track and classify small flying objects such as birds, bats and drones. It sells them to aviation, defence, security and ecology teams that want a full view of their airspace. Its two main products are IRIS, a 3D drone radar in a 29 kg package, and MAX, a 3D bird detection radar.

IRIS uses micro-doppler classification and deep neural network technology to distinguish blades and rotating parts. It combines 360 degree views, 60 degree elevation and a 5 km instrumented range. A software-only update, Long-Range Mode, lets operators switch between 5 km and 12 km instrumented ranges in minutes. MAX pairs with two software interfaces, Bird Viewer for live airspace and Report Viewer for historical analysis. Airports, airfields and wind farms use the bird and bat radars to react to hazards as they emerge.

The name comes from a 1980 project by the Dutch research institute TNO to prevent bird strikes on Royal Netherlands Air Force planes. Siete Hamminga, now CEO, spun the technology out of TNO in 2010 to found the company. It reports more than 300 radars deployed worldwide and a staff of 150 or more people. In 2024 its shareholders reached an acquisition agreement with the Dutch investment company Parcom. Scarecrow, a maker of bird dispersal and data logging systems based on bio-acoustic technology, is a Robin company.
